bull_bear.body:
- Captive coal mines (Moher and Moher Amlohri Extension) supply Sasan UMPP's fuel requirement, giving fuel security and cost competitiveness
- Sasan UMPP is one of the largest integrated coal-based power plants globally and ran at a Plant Load Factor of ~87% against an all-India average thermal PLF of approximately 60%
- Long-term power offtake arrangements and long-term fuel supply arrangements underpin generation reliability
- Standalone bank debt-free status achieved through continued deleveraging and asset monetisation, improving financial flexibility
- Operating experience across diversified solar technologies (PV and solar thermal/CSP) supporting the renewable build-out
- Secured large dispatchable renewable pipeline (solar plus BESS) with SECI and SJVN, positioning the company in India's energy transition
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Material uncertainty related to going concern — corporate guarantee invoked and insolvency proceedings initiated against the Company — The auditors draw attention to Note 28 of the standalone financial statements: the lender of Samalkot Power Limited, a wholly owned subsidiary, has invoked the corporate guarantee against the Company and demanded payment of overdue dues, and has initiated the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process against the Company under section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. The auditors state these events and conditions indicate a material uncertainty that may cast significant doubt on the Company's ability to continue as a going concern, although the accounts have been prepared on a going-concern basis and the opinion is not modified in respect of the matter.
- Enforcement Directorate proceedings under PMLA, including asset attachment and prosecution of the Company, subsidiaries and employees — The auditors' Emphasis of Matters draws attention to Note 33(a) describing ongoing proceedings initiated by the Directorate of Enforcement under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002. The Directors' Report records search and seizure by ED, the arrest of the former Executive Director and CFO in the matter of an alleged false bank guarantee submitted to SECI, a supplementary prosecution complaint against the Company, two subsidiaries and two employees, an FIR by the Economic Offences Wing of Delhi Police on a SECI complaint, and provisional attachment of certain assets of the Company and its subsidiaries, confirmed after year-end by the Adjudicating Authority for 365 days. The Company states it and its employees acted bona-fidely and are victims of fraud, forgery, cheating and conspiracy by third parties.
- SEBI enforcement exposure — two Show Cause Notices and a SEBI-initiated forensic audit — A Show Cause Notice dated September 30, 2025 alleges violations of the SEBI (Prohibition of Fraudulent and Unfair Trade Practices) Regulations, 2003 read with the SEBI Act, 1992; a further Show Cause Notice dated April 10, 2026 alleges violations of Regulation 30 and Regulations 4(1)(c) and 4(1)(e) of the Listing Regulations; and SEBI, by letter dated January 14, 2026, initiated a forensic audit of the Company in connection with alleged violations of the SEBI Act, the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act and the Companies Act.
- Regulatory and tariff-recovery risk in a heavily regulated power sector — The BRSR material-issues table identifies Regulatory Issues as both an opportunity and a risk: the power sector and the Company's projects are heavily regulated in terms of operations and tariff recoveries, and the Company is engaged with State and Central regulators for adjudication of various disputes with power procurers, which could have positive or negative implications for operations. Mitigation is limited to advocacy through industry associations.
- Environmental emissions and ash disposal from thermal generation, with penalty exposure on non-compliance — The BRSR material-issues table flags that thermal power generation entails emissions of SOx, NOx and CO2 and the need to dispose of large quantities of ash, and that failure to comply with the norms could lead to negative impact and penalties. The Company states it operates well within approved emission parameters.
- Workforce safety and labour relations at project sites — The BRSR table records that the nature of the business is subject to high risk of safety hazards, mitigated through regular safety training for employees and third-party contract workers plus periodic safety audits and inspections; and separately that any incident at a project or industrial action by workers can lead to operational disruptions. The scale is material — the Company reports 6,321 other-than-permanent workers against 1,278 permanent employees.
- Cyber security risk to information systems — The BRSR table identifies the risk of security breaches gaining access to information systems due to internet exposure, mitigated by an Integrated Intrusion Detection and Prevention Monitoring System with auto monitoring, log monitoring, security patch monitoring and alerting, encryption of incoming and outgoing communication, and employee awareness campaigns.
- Board and senior-management instability, including the loss of the CFO to arrest — The Directors' Report records an unusually heavy churn in FY26: the Executive Director and CFO resigned on October 11, 2025 due to his arrest and pending investigation, with the CEO given additional charge as interim CFO; two directors resigned with effect from August 29, 2025 and another on November 03, 2025; several additional directors were appointed during and after the year; and thirteen Board meetings were held during the financial year. The Company also concentrates the CEO and CFO roles in one person, and the statutory auditors are changing at the ensuing AGM.
bull_bear.title: Bear — key risks

business.body: Reliance Power develops, constructs and operates power generation projects in India, supported by integrated captive coal resources and long-term power offtake arrangements. Its portfolio is predominantly large-scale coal-based thermal generation, complemented by solar PV, concentrated solar and wind assets. Its customers are power distribution companies, which in turn supply power to end consumers.

- Transition toward the renewable energy space, adding large-scale solar generation paired with Battery Energy Storage Systems through wholly-owned subsidiaries (Reliance NU Suntech, Reliance NU Energies)

outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: Reliance Power operates an installed generation capacity of 5,305 MW as of FY 2025-26, predominantly large-scale thermal, and is advancing an energy transition built around large-scale solar paired with Battery Energy Storage Systems. Under development, the Company states it has secured a 930 MW solar + 465 MW / 1,860 MWh BESS project, a 350 MW solar + 175 MW / 700 MWh BESS project and a 650 MW solar + 750 MW / 3,300 MWh BESS project, described as a significant step towards dispatchable renewable energy solutions. The 930 MW award sits with wholly-owned subsidiary Reliance NU Suntech Private Limited, which has signed a PPA with SECI and will deploy more than 1,700 MWp of solar generation capacity to achieve the contracted 930 MW; separately, wholly-owned subsidiary Reliance NU Energies Private Limited has been awarded two renewable projects by SJVN aggregating about 1,500 MWp of solar and 4,000 MWh of BESS. Internationally, Reliance Bangladesh LNG and Power Limited's 718 MW (net) plant at Meghnaghat near Dhaka, executed with strategic partner JERA Power International (Netherlands), commenced commercial operations in July 2025; and Reliance Enterprise Private Limited with Druk Holdings and Investment will jointly develop Bhutan's largest solar project, a 500 MW 50:50 venture, with announced plans to also jointly develop a 770 MW hydroelectric project (the associate Reliance Enterprises Private Limited having formed the JV GDL - Reliance Solar Pte Ltd in Bhutan with Green Digital Private Limited, a State Owned Enterprise of the Royal Government of Bhutan). On the other side of the portfolio, the non-operational gas-based Samalkot Power Project is earmarked for a planned exit under the Company's portfolio-optimisation and disciplined capital-allocation strategy. No commissioning dates or rupee capex quantum are stated anywhere in the routed text.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: Reliance Power operates an installed generation capacity of 5,305 MW as of FY 2025-26, predominantly large-scale thermal, and is advancing an energy transition built around large-scale solar paired with Battery Energy Storage Systems. Under development, the Company states it has secured a 930 MW solar + 465 MW / 1,860 MWh BESS project, a 350 MW solar + 175 MW / 700 MWh BESS project and a 650 MW solar + 750 MW / 3,300 MWh BESS project, described as a significant step towards dispatchable renewable energy solutions. The 930 MW award sits with wholly-owned subsidiary Reliance NU Suntech Private Limited, which has signed a PPA with SECI and will deploy more than 1,700 MWp of solar generation capacity to achieve the contracted 930 MW; separately, wholly-owned subsidiary Reliance NU Energies Private Limited has been awarded two renewable projects by SJVN aggregating about 1,500 MWp of solar and 4,000 MWh of BESS. Internationally, Reliance Bangladesh LNG and Power Limited's 718 MW (net) plant at Meghnaghat near Dhaka, executed with strategic partner JERA Power International (Netherlands), commenced commercial operations in July 2025; and Reliance Enterprise Private Limited with Druk Holdings and Investment will jointly develop Bhutan's largest solar project, a 500 MW 50:50 venture, with announced plans to also jointly develop a 770 MW hydroelectric project (the associate Reliance Enterprises Private Limited having formed the JV GDL - Reliance Solar Pte Ltd in Bhutan with Green Digital Private Limited, a State Owned Enterprise of the Royal Government of Bhutan). On the other side of the portfolio, the non-operational gas-based Samalkot Power Project is earmarked for a planned exit under the Company's portfolio-optimisation and disciplined capital-allocation strategy. No commissioning dates or rupee capex quantum are stated anywhere in the routed text.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Captive coal mines (Moher and Moher Amlohri Extension) supply Sasan UMPP's fuel requirement, giving fuel security and cost competitiveness
- Sasan UMPP is one of the largest integrated coal-based power plants globally and ran at a Plant Load Factor of ~87% against an all-India average thermal PLF of approximately 60%
- Long-term power offtake arrangements and long-term fuel supply arrangements underpin generation reliability
- Standalone bank debt-free status achieved through continued deleveraging and asset monetisation, improving financial flexibility
- Operating experience across diversified solar technologies (PV and solar thermal/CSP) supporting the renewable build-out
- Secured large dispatchable renewable pipeline (solar plus BESS) with SECI and SJVN, positioning the company in India's energy transition

risks.title: Bear — key risks
risks.body:
- Material uncertainty related to going concern — corporate guarantee invoked and insolvency proceedings initiated against the Company — The auditors draw attention to Note 28 of the standalone financial statements: the lender of Samalkot Power Limited, a wholly owned subsidiary, has invoked the corporate guarantee against the Company and demanded payment of overdue dues, and has initiated the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process against the Company under section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. The auditors state these events and conditions indicate a material uncertainty that may cast significant doubt on the Company's ability to continue as a going concern, although the accounts have been prepared on a going-concern basis and the opinion is not modified in respect of the matter.
- Enforcement Directorate proceedings under PMLA, including asset attachment and prosecution of the Company, subsidiaries and employees — The auditors' Emphasis of Matters draws attention to Note 33(a) describing ongoing proceedings initiated by the Directorate of Enforcement under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002. The Directors' Report records search and seizure by ED, the arrest of the former Executive Director and CFO in the matter of an alleged false bank guarantee submitted to SECI, a supplementary prosecution complaint against the Company, two subsidiaries and two employees, an FIR by the Economic Offences Wing of Delhi Police on a SECI complaint, and provisional attachment of certain assets of the Company and its subsidiaries, confirmed after year-end by the Adjudicating Authority for 365 days. The Company states it and its employees acted bona-fidely and are victims of fraud, forgery, cheating and conspiracy by third parties.
- SEBI enforcement exposure — two Show Cause Notices and a SEBI-initiated forensic audit — A Show Cause Notice dated September 30, 2025 alleges violations of the SEBI (Prohibition of Fraudulent and Unfair Trade Practices) Regulations, 2003 read with the SEBI Act, 1992; a further Show Cause Notice dated April 10, 2026 alleges violations of Regulation 30 and Regulations 4(1)(c) and 4(1)(e) of the Listing Regulations; and SEBI, by letter dated January 14, 2026, initiated a forensic audit of the Company in connection with alleged violations of the SEBI Act, the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act and the Companies Act.
- Regulatory and tariff-recovery risk in a heavily regulated power sector — The BRSR material-issues table identifies Regulatory Issues as both an opportunity and a risk: the power sector and the Company's projects are heavily regulated in terms of operations and tariff recoveries, and the Company is engaged with State and Central regulators for adjudication of various disputes with power procurers, which could have positive or negative implications for operations. Mitigation is limited to advocacy through industry associations.
- Environmental emissions and ash disposal from thermal generation, with penalty exposure on non-compliance — The BRSR material-issues table flags that thermal power generation entails emissions of SOx, NOx and CO2 and the need to dispose of large quantities of ash, and that failure to comply with the norms could lead to negative impact and penalties. The Company states it operates well within approved emission parameters.
- Workforce safety and labour relations at project sites — The BRSR table records that the nature of the business is subject to high risk of safety hazards, mitigated through regular safety training for employees and third-party contract workers plus periodic safety audits and inspections; and separately that any incident at a project or industrial action by workers can lead to operational disruptions. The scale is material — the Company reports 6,321 other-than-permanent workers against 1,278 permanent employees.
- Cyber security risk to information systems — The BRSR table identifies the risk of security breaches gaining access to information systems due to internet exposure, mitigated by an Integrated Intrusion Detection and Prevention Monitoring System with auto monitoring, log monitoring, security patch monitoring and alerting, encryption of incoming and outgoing communication, and employee awareness campaigns.
- Board and senior-management instability, including the loss of the CFO to arrest — The Directors' Report records an unusually heavy churn in FY26: the Executive Director and CFO resigned on October 11, 2025 due to his arrest and pending investigation, with the CEO given additional charge as interim CFO; two directors resigned with effect from August 29, 2025 and another on November 03, 2025; several additional directors were appointed during and after the year; and thirteen Board meetings were held during the financial year. The Company also concentrates the CEO and CFO roles in one person, and the statutory auditors are changing at the ensuing AGM.
